title: Retail media creative specs, rules and production tips
summary: Retail media creative best practices for Amazon, Walmart Connect, Instacart and more, plus the specs, rules and production system to scale on-brand variants.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


Retail media creative gets about one second to sell, often with the sound off and right next to competitors, and every network from Amazon to Roundel has its own specs. The assets that win lead with the product in the first frame, make one claim and stay recognizable at thumbnail size, while the five failure modes (repurposed brand films, relying on sound, hero-shot habits, ignoring product order and quality slipping at volume) quietly drain performance. Scaling it takes variant automation, a brand system like Brand Brain and custom AI image models working together, and Superside's work with Amazon Home and Colgate-Palmolive shows what that looks like at volume.


Retail media gives brands a direct line to high-intent shoppers. It also hands creative teams a workload most of them weren't built for: a high volume of assets for multiple networks, every month, each with its own rules. No wonder so many teams already feel[stretched to breaking point](https://www.superside.com/blog/breakpoint) .


Adding more people rarely fixes it. **The better fix is a system that helps creative teams get the specs right, stay on brief and hold quality as volume climbs.**


Most retail media articles focus on where to buy and how to bid. This guide covers what happens after that decision: the creative assets teams need to produce at scale and how to simplify that process.


## The budget moved. The teams didn't keep up.


The case for retail media is no longer in question. eMarketer projects US commerce media ad spending will[reach $142.07 billion and account for 23.9% of all digital ad spending by 2030](https://www.emarketer.com/content/commerce-media-ad-spending-forecast-2026) . It also forecasts that Amazon's retail media revenues alone will[exceed $75 billion by 2028](https://www.emarketer.com/content/retail-media-ad-spending-forecast-h1-2026) .


But spending charts hide what happens behind the scenes. **When budgets flood into a dozen retail media networks, the creative burden doesn't grow linearly. It explodes.**


Each network has its own ad formats, ratios, character limits and content rules. Each placement behaves differently. Retail media assets also need constant refreshing, because ad fatigue quickly chips away at[creative performance](https://www.superside.com/blog/what-is-creative-performance) .


Multiply networks by placements by variants by refresh cycles and you get the real work behind retail media advertising: a production problem measured in thousands of assets.


Many brands still plan retail media around the media buy, then ask their creative teams to keep up. That gets the order wrong. **Retail media is a creative production problem with a media budget attached, not the other way around.** For the bigger picture, our roundup of[advertising creative trends](https://www.superside.com/blog/advertising-creative-trends) is a useful primer.


## 4 jobs every retail media asset has to do


Retail media creative works in advertising's most hostile environment: the moment of purchase, surrounded by competitors, in front of a task-focused shopper who's moving fast.


Many brands optimize for one or two of these jobs. **If you don't account for all four from the start, performance suffers.**


1. **Sell, don't impress:** Capture attention quickly and give shoppers a reason to buy. Think legible, product-forward creative that turns attention into "add to cart."
2. **Win attention fast:** In a piece for[The Drum](https://www.thedrum.com/industry-insight/2026-the-year-creative-claims-its-rightful-place-in-retail-media) , Co-op's Anthony Jackson pointed to research putting the in-store moment at around one second in a convenience store and just 0.4 seconds in a supermarket. Focus on a clear one-second pitch and keep the creative ruthlessly simple.
3. **Work with the sound off:** Many video placements start muted or don't support audio at all. The product, message and branding should be clear from the visuals and on-screen text alone.
4. **Sequence products deliberately:** In multi-product formats, position matters. Instacart says shoppers are most likely to engage with[the first product that appears](https://company.instacart.com/instacart-ads/shoppable-display-ads-best-practice) in a shoppable display ad.


Olivia McCullagh, Retail Media Lead at IAB UK, explained in the same Drum piece why purpose-built creative matters more than ever:


With stronger evidence linking creative to performance (and AI driving greater uniformity), distinctive, context-aware work is becoming the key differentiator.


Olivia McCullagh


Retail Media Lead, IAB UK


## Network by network: A quick primer


Today's top retail media networks may look similar from the outside, but their creative requirements vary widely. **Specs change often, so always confirm the live requirements for your exact placement before production starts.**


Here's a closer look at six major platforms, popular ad formats and what creative teams need to consider.


### 1. Amazon Ads


Amazon's advertising services brought in[$17.2 billion in Q1 2026](https://ir.aboutamazon.com/news-release/news-release-details/2026/Amazon-com-Announces-First-Quarter-Results/default.aspx) . That scale makes it impossible to ignore.


**Sponsored Products video:** According to[Amazon's own guide](https://advertising.amazon.com/library/guides/sponsored-products-video) , campaigns with video see 67% higher click-through rates (CTR) and a 9% higher conversion rate than campaigns without it. For the 20% of shoppers who watch beyond five seconds, CTR jumps eightfold, and those viewers are twice as likely to buy from that brand within seven days.


The rules are strict. Videos must run at least seven seconds and don't support audio. The product should fill at least half of the frame, and blurry frames, slideshows, letterboxing, excessive motion graphics and talking-head videos are all out.


**Sponsored Brands video:**[Amazon's specs](https://advertising.amazon.com/resources/ad-specs/sponsored-brands-video) call for videos between 6 and 45 seconds (20 seconds or less highly recommended) in a 16:9 ratio only. By default, these videos always start without audio.


**What this means for creative teams:** Make the product dominate the frame, focus on features and use and make sure the message works entirely without sound. Our Q&A on[how to advertise on Amazon](https://www.superside.com/blog/how-to-advertise-on-amazon) with former Amazon ad leaders goes deeper on platform craft.


### 2. Walmart Connect


Walmart Connect reaches approximately 150 million US customers every week across digital and physical touchpoints. Its[CES 2026 update](https://www.walmartconnect.com/resources/articles/2026/ces-2026-key-themes) shows how quickly the network has expanded beyond sponsored search.


**Walmart's own Automated Creative Generator can reduce advertisers' median creative production time by up to 80%** , according to the same update. Read that as a signal from the network itself that creative volume is the bottleneck.


[Sponsored Videos](https://www.walmartconnect.com/solutions/sponsored-videos) run between 5 and 45 seconds. Walmart Connect is also pushing further into CTV, noting that adding Walmart Connect CTV or VIZIO to linear TV buys reached audiences three-quarters of whom weren't reached through linear TV alone.


**What this means for creative teams:** Front-load the product and message, because there's little room for a slow build. The same campaign may also need separate creative for Walmart's CTV and other environments.


### 3. Instacart


Instacart calls its network[the largest grocery ad ecosystem](https://company.instacart.com/ads) , reaching 55+ million consumers across 100,000 storefronts on Instacart Marketplace plus 310+ retail media networks and popular marketplaces.


Its shoppable display ads feature a carousel of pinned products. Because shoppers are most likely to engage with the first product, Instacart recommends pinning your highest-performing, most widely available item first.


**What this means for creative teams:** Don't simply lead with the newest SKU or the prettiest pack shot. Choose the product most likely to perform and be in stock across retailers.


### 4. Kroger Precision Marketing


Kroger Precision Marketing (KPM) uses first-party retail data from[60+ million US households](https://www.krogerprecisionmarketing.com/knowledge-hub/blog/84-51-data-science-and-retail-analytics-in-action/) to power targeting and measurement across its retail media network.


KPM publishes separate[creative specs and policy documents](https://www.krogerprecisionmarketing.com/resources/specs/) for each format, and some of its display ads can run with or without added Kroger branding.


**What this means for creative teams:** Build to the exact placement and template, and check which brand elements the format already handles before you bake them into the artwork.


### 5. Roundel


[Roundel](https://roundel.com/) uses first-party data from 100M+ Target Circle members to reach and understand Target shoppers.


The network spans several buying and creative models. Display runs as a managed service across Target properties and 150+ premium publishers, programmatic is self-service through your own DSP and social spans Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest and Snapchat.


**What this means for creative teams:** Confirm the placement and service model before production starts. A Roundel campaign may need different builds for Target.com, external publishers and social platforms.


### 6. Criteo


Criteo isn't a retailer-owned media network. Instead, it's part of the infrastructure connecting the wider retail media ecosystem, with[4,000+ brands and 200+ retailers](https://www.criteo.com/solutions/retail-media/) using its retail media solutions worldwide.


Through[Commerce Max](https://www.criteo.com/platform/commerce-max/) , you can plan, buy and measure ads across hundreds of retailers and premium publishers from one place. That reduces platform fragmentation, but not creative complexity. For sponsored products, for example, Criteo uses the creative from the retailer's organic product listing.


**What this means for creative teams:** Centralized media buying doesn't remove production work. Your product listings and imagery need to be strong at every retailer, and you may still need retailer- and placement-specific assets.


### Why fragmentation is now an industry problem


**Perhaps the clearest sign of how costly fragmentation has become is that the industry is trying to standardize it.**


In January 2026,[IAB Europe released its Flexi Ad Sizes Guidelines](https://iabeurope.eu/knowledge_hub/iab-europe-flexi-ad-sizes-guidelines-for-retail-media-networks/) , created in collaboration with Tesco Media. The guidelines recommend four flexible aspect ratios for static display ads, with the aim of[faster activation and fewer custom builds](https://iabeurope.eu/retail-media-spotlight-kicking-off-2026-with-new-standards-smarter-creative-and-strong-momentum/) .


Until standards like these are widely adopted, brands still have to manage the fragmentation themselves, ideally with a system for[content localization](https://www.superside.com/blog/content-localization) and versioning rather than heroic manual effort.


## On-site, off-site and in-store have different requirements


Retail media creative needs to work across three very different environments:


- **On-site retail media:** Appears on a retailer's own digital properties, such as its website or app.
- **Off-site retail media:** Uses retailer data to reach shoppers on external channels, such as social platforms, publisher sites and connected TV.
- **In-store advertising:** Reaches shoppers inside physical stores through digital screens and other in-store placements.


The challenge isn't only adapting creative to each environment. **It's making those experiences feel connected.**


Stacy Gratz, Revenue and Growth Director at Tesco Media, calls this "compound creativity," meaning consistent, context-based storytelling across in-store, online and offsite. As she told The Drum, "When creativity compounds, impact multiplies."


Each environment reaches shoppers in a different context, though, so the same creative won't work equally well across all three:


Surface Shopper context and intent What the creative must do


On-site High intent; actively shopping on a retailer's site or app Be product-forward, clear and easy to act on


Off-site Lower intent; reached outside the retailer's own properties Carry enough brand and product context to make sense away from the retailer


In-store digital displays Passive; shopping inside a physical store Communicate quickly and clearly in a busy in-store environment


Treating retail media as a single channel makes it easy to miss these differences. A better approach is to build creative for each environment. In that sense, retail media is as much an[omnichannel design](https://www.superside.com/blog/omnichannel-design-partners) challenge as a media-buying one, and it's closely tied to how your brand shows up in[DTC](https://www.superside.com/blog/dtc-branding-examples) .


## What effective retail media creative looks like


Strip away the network differences and the assets that perform share a short list of traits. Here's what to double-check before your campaigns go live.


### 1. The first frame does the work


Assume the shopper sees one frame and nothing else. **The product, brand and reason to click should all be clear immediately.**


For many teams, that means flipping the usual creative hierarchy, which often builds toward a reveal.


### 2. The product is unmistakable at thumbnail size


Shrink your asset to thumbnail size and look at it on a phone. If the pack isn't identifiable, go back to the drawing board.


Category cues often matter more than brand cues here, because shoppers scan for the shape and color of what they're looking for before they read anything. Strong[packaging design](https://www.superside.com/blog/packaging-designs) does a lot of this work for you.


### 3. You make one strong, clear claim


Strong retail media assets carry a single message well. Pick the one claim most likely to trigger an "add to cart," whether that's price, format, a new variant or a benefit. Then let everything else go.


## 5 failure modes that weaken retail media creative


The same production pressures keep showing up in enterprise teams, and they create predictable problems in retail media.


Here are five failure modes to watch for, plus the practical fix for each:


Failure mode Why it happens The fix


Repurposing brand assets Reusing campaign creative instead of adapting it to the placement Build for the specific network, format and placement


Relying on sound Treating voiceover or music as essential to the message Make sure the core message works visually and through on-screen text


Designing around the hero shot Prioritizing the main campaign image over clear product info and legibility Make the product easy to recognize at the size and context where it appears


Ignoring product order Treating product sequence as an afterthought in multi-product formats Put the strongest product first


Letting quality slip at volume Producing large numbers of variants manually under deadline Use a repeatable production system with built-in brand rules


**The last failure mode can be the most damaging.** As teams produce more variants under tight deadlines, small inconsistencies creep in. Over time, they weaken brand recognition and trust.


The broader lesson is to design for the specific medium and platform, and to back that work with an operating model that holds quality and consistency as volume grows. Our guides to[designing high-performing ads](https://www.superside.com/blog/design-high-performing-ads) and[A/B testing your designs](https://www.superside.com/blog/a-b-testing-your-designs) are good next reads.


## The always-on refresh problem


Retail media creative often stays live for a long time. However, as products, offers and performance shift, you need to update, test and refresh your assets.


Two things make this difficult. First, seasonality and peak moments like[Black Friday and Cyber Monday](https://www.superside.com/blog/make-black-friday-cyber-monday-ads) can make asset demand spike. Second, repeated exposure to the same ad throughout the shopping journey reduces its effectiveness.


**That makes measurement part of production.** Your creative and marketing teams need to know which variants are still performing, which are tiring and where to iterate next.[Creative performance benchmarking](https://www.superside.com/blog/creative-performance-benchmarking-measurement) and[data-informed creative decisions](https://www.superside.com/blog/data-creative-performance) help guide this process and keep[performance marketing quality](https://www.superside.com/blog/performance-marketing-quality) high.


The operational challenge is keeping that cycle moving week after week. That's why some brands supplement their in-house teams with[ad creative agencies](https://www.superside.com/blog/ad-creative-agencies) ,[creative performance partners](https://www.superside.com/blog/creative-performance-agencies) and[packaging design agencies](https://www.superside.com/blog/packaging-design-agencies) .


## How to brief retail media creative


Retail media creative depends heavily on context. The same idea may need to work across different placements, formats, shopper missions and retailer rules, so a generic campaign brief usually isn't enough.


**A useful retail media brief gives the creative team everything it needs to build for the exact environments you're targeting.** Five details belong in every one of these[creative briefs](https://www.superside.com/blog/creative-briefs-production) :


1. **The exact placement, not only the channel:** "Amazon" isn't a brief. "Sponsored Products video, sound off, appearing in these search placements for these terms" is.
2. **The competitive context:** Consider what will sit next to this asset on the page. A creative decision that looks bold in isolation can disappear in a grid of similar packaging.
3. **What the shopper is trying to do:** Someone searching a category term has a different goal from someone reordering a familiar brand. The creative should reflect that.
4. **Every required variation upfront:** Specify the sizes, ratios, languages, products and other versions you'll need before production starts. This gives the team a clear variant matrix and avoids late-stage additions.
5. **Refresh expectations:** State whether this is a one-off campaign or the first in a rolling series, because that affects how modular and reusable the creative should be.


Getting these details into the brief prevents many of the production problems covered earlier.

Producing every size, ratio and placement variant by hand is where budgets and timelines die.[Automated ad creative versioning](https://www.superside.com/blog/automate-ad-creative-versioning) turns one master concept into the full matrix of network-compliant variants. **Automation without a strong brand system just means your team produces off-brand work faster.**

## FAQs


Retail media is advertising powered by retailers and their shopper data, running on retailer-owned properties and other channels such as off-site media and in-store screens. Retail media creative is the set of assets built for those placements. Because it reaches shoppers close to the point of purchase, it needs to be clear, product-forward and adapted to each network, placement and format.


There's no single set of retail media ad specs, because requirements vary by network, placement and format. Amazon Sponsored Brands video, for example, calls for 6 to 45 seconds in a 16:9 ratio. Always check the live specs for your exact placement before production begins. The industry is working toward more consistency, with[IAB Europe's 2026 Flexi Ad Sizes Guidelines](https://iabeurope.eu/knowledge_hub/iab-europe-flexi-ad-sizes-guidelines-for-retail-media-networks/) recommending four flexible aspect ratios for static display.


More than most teams expect. Multiply the number of networks by placements, product and message variants and refresh cycles, and you quickly reach hundreds or thousands of assets. That's why variant automation plus a brand system is what makes quality control at scale possible.


In most cases, yes. Amazon Sponsored Brands videos start without audio by default, and Sponsored Products videos don't support audio at all. Design the core message to work through visuals and on-screen text first, and treat audio as a bonus where it's supported.


With a brand system rather than manual checks. When teams produce at volume under deadline, consistency breaks unless brand rules travel with every asset. An AI context engine like Brand Brain carries your guidelines into every brief and checks deliverables, so automation speeds production without multiplying off-brand work.


AI is well suited to the repetitive, high-volume parts. Custom AI image models trained on a brand's products generate shelf-ready imagery much faster, and automation turns a master concept into the full set of compliant variants. But AI works best inside a brand system and under human creative direction, so speed doesn't cost you consistency or quality.
